summary: Before a client can use TLS Encrypted ClientHello (ECH), it must learn the server's ECH configuration. This specification describes how to publish that configuration in DNS using SVCB or HTTPS resource records, so clients can fetch it before connecting.

plainLanguage.summary: Encrypted ClientHello hides the name of the site a browser is visiting from anyone watching the connection, but the browser has to look up that site's encryption settings first. This document says where the server puts those settings: in the DNS record for its name, in a parameter called ech. The browser reads that record before it starts the connection, and it must not quietly fall back to an unprotected connection when the record is there.

subtitle: How a server publishes its Encrypted ClientHello settings in DNS so clients can find them before connecting.

tldr.problem: Encrypted ClientHello hides the name of the server a client is contacting, but the client has to know the server's encryption configuration before it can send an encrypted hello. If that configuration is not published somewhere the client can find, the protection cannot be used.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9848 defines a new service parameter, ech, for SVCB and HTTPS DNS records. Its value is the server's ECH configuration, base 64 encoded for presentation. A client looks the record up, and only then sends a ClientHello, and it must not fall back to an unprotected connection when every endpoint offers the parameter.
tldr.outcome: The document registers SvcParamKey 5 for ech and sets the rules for servers, clients and HTTP Alt-Svc. It also explains the limits: a record set that mixes endpoints with and without ech can be downgraded, and the real name still appears in the DNS query.

facts.label: Guess probability
facts.value: At least 1/K, where K is the size of the anonymity set

today: RFC 9848 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2026, and it has not been obsoleted. IANA has updated the DNS SVCB Service Parameter Keys registry so that SvcParamKey 5 is named ech and refers to this document. The Encrypted ClientHello mechanism it bootstraps is defined in RFC 9849.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Service Bindings framework lets server operators publish a detailed description of their service in the Domain Name System, using SVCB or HTTPS records. Each SVCB record describes a single alternative endpoint and holds a collection of service parameters, which can be extended with new kinds of information. Clients use those parameters to improve the privacy, security and performance of their connection to the endpoint.

This document defines a new service parameter that enables the use of TLS Encrypted ClientHello in TLS-based protocols. It can be used in SVCB records, HTTPS records, or any future SVCB-compatible DNS records, and it is intended to serve as the primary bootstrap mechanism for Encrypted ClientHello. The Encrypted ClientHello specification itself is RFC 9849.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNS record can carry extra information about a service, and clients use it to set up a better connection. This document adds one such piece of information: the encryption settings a client needs in order to hide the name of the server inside the first message of a TLS handshake.

sections.title: The ech Service Parameter
sections.content:
The ech parameter key conveys the Encrypted ClientHello configuration of an alternative endpoint. It applies to all schemes that use TLS-based protocols, including DTLS and QUIC version 1, unless otherwise specified.

In wire format, the value of the parameter is an ECHConfigList, including the redundant length prefix. In presentation format, which is how it appears in a zone file, the value is that ECHConfigList in Base 64 encoding. Base 64 is used to simplify integration with TLS server software. To enable simpler parsing, the parameter must not contain escape sequences.

The example given in the document is an ech parameter whose configuration has a public name of ech-sites.example.net:

ech="AEj+DQBEAQAgACAdd+scUi0IYFsXnUIU7ko2Nd9+F8M26pAGZVpz/KrWPgAEAAEAAWQVZWNoLXNpdGVzLmV4YW1wbGUubmV0AAA="
sections.plainLanguage: The parameter's value is the server's encryption configuration, which is a list of one or more entries. In a zone file it is written as Base 64 text so that it can be copied straight into server software without being re-encoded.

sections.title: Requirements for Server Deployments
sections.content:
When publishing a record containing an ech parameter, the publisher must ensure that all the IP addresses of the target name correspond to servers that have access to the corresponding private key or are authoritative for the public name. Otherwise the connections fail entirely.

These servers should support a protocol version that is compatible with Encrypted ClientHello. At the time of writing, the compatible versions are TLS 1.3, DTLS 1.3 and QUIC version 1. If the server does not support a compatible version, each connection attempt has to be retried, which delays the connection and wastes resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Every address the record points at must be a server that can actually decrypt the client's first message, or one that is the authority for the name the client is hiding. If that does not hold, the connection simply fails. The server must also speak a version of TLS that supports the encryption, or every connection attempt has to be tried again.

sections.title: Requirements for Client Implementations
sections.content:
Section 5.1 deals with fallback. The SVCB-optional client behaviour permits a client to fall back to a direct connection if all the SVCB options fail. That is not suitable for Encrypted ClientHello, because a fallback would cancel out the privacy benefit. A client that supports Encrypted ClientHello and uses SVCB-optional mode must therefore switch to SVCB-reliant connection establishment if SVCB resolution succeeded and all the alternative endpoints have an ech parameter.

Section 5.2 covers the ClientHello. When Encrypted ClientHello is in use, the TLS ClientHello is divided into an unencrypted outer ClientHello and an encrypted inner ClientHello. The outer ClientHello is an implementation detail of Encrypted ClientHello, and its contents are controlled by the ECH configuration. The inner ClientHello is used for establishing the connection to the service, so its contents may be influenced by the other service parameters. For example, the requirements on Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation identifiers apply only to the inner ClientHello, and it is the inner ClientHello whose Server Name Indication identifies the desired service.

Section 5.3 covers performance. Before the client retrieves the SVCB records it does not know whether they contain an ech parameter, so as a latency optimization clients may prefetch DNS records that will only be used if the parameter is absent, which is the case only in SVCB-optional mode. Because the ech parameter alters the contents of the TLS ClientHello when it is present, clients that support Encrypted ClientHello must not issue any TLS ClientHello until SVCB resolution has completed.
sections.plainLanguage: Three rules govern the client. It must not fall back to a plain connection when the record said the server supports the encryption, because that would defeat the purpose. The name of the service goes only in the inner, encrypted part of the hello, never in the outer part. And the client must finish its DNS lookup before it sends the hello at all, so that it knows whether the hello has to be encrypted.

sections.title: Interaction with HTTP Alt-Svc
sections.content:
HTTP clients that implement both HTTP Alt-Svc and the HTTPS record type can use them together, provided that they only perform connection attempts that are consistent with both sets of parameters. At the time of writing there is no defined parameter related to Encrypted ClientHello for Alt-Svc, so a connection attempt that uses Encrypted ClientHello is considered consistent with an Alt-Svc field value that does not mention it.

Origins that publish an ech parameter in their HTTPS record should also publish an HTTPS record with the ech parameter for every alt-authority offered in their Alt-Svc field values. Otherwise clients might reveal the name of the server in an unencrypted ClientHello to an alt-authority.

If all the HTTPS records for an alt-authority contain ech parameters, the client must adopt SVCB-reliant behaviour for that record set. This rules out some connections that Alt-Svc would otherwise allow.
sections.plainLanguage: Alt-Svc lets a server point clients at a different host. If a server uses it, it must publish the same encryption parameter for each of the alternative hosts it names, otherwise a client would send the real name in the clear to one of them. When every record for an alternative host carries the parameter, the client must not fall back to a plain connection for that host either.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The document gives six example zones. The first places the same configuration on the apex of a zone and on a web name, with an HTTPS record carrying an ech parameter at each, and it notes that the zone is compatible with clients that do or do not support HTTPS records.

The second example describes a service that lets clients choose between two pools of servers, each with its own ECH configuration, using two SVCB records that point at the two pools and carry different ech values.

The third example is an aliasing-based content delivery network. The CDN operator's zone holds the pool with the ech parameter, and the customer's zone holds an HTTPS record that aliases to that pool, with apex address records kept for clients that do not support HTTPS records.

The fourth example is a domain that is only reachable using Encrypted ClientHello. The HTTPS record names a backend, carries the ech parameter, and adds the mandatory parameter, which tells the client that it must not connect without Encrypted ClientHello.

The fifth example is a multi-CDN configuration using server-side selection, with two versions of the customer's zone pointing at two different CDN operators' pools, each with its own ech value. The last example is a DNS server zone where the ech parameter is published alongside the Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation and DoH path parameters, at the apex and at a _dns name with a SVCB record.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the parameter being used in several ways. A single server can publish it at one name; two server pools behind one name can each publish their own, so the client picks one; a content delivery network can publish it in its own zone and let the customer's zone point there; and a domain that must never be contacted in the clear marks the parameter as mandatory, which tells the client not to try without it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A record set containing some records with an ech parameter and some without is vulnerable to a downgrade attack. A network intermediary can block connections to the endpoints that support Encrypted ClientHello, causing the client to fall back to an endpoint without it. This configuration is not recommended, but it may be unavoidable when combining endpoints from different providers or during a staged rollout. Zone owners who do use a mixed configuration should mark the records with ech as more preferred, that is, with a lower SvcPriority value, than those without, to maximize the likelihood that Encrypted ClientHello is used in the absence of an active adversary.

When Encrypted ClientHello is deployed, the inner TLS Server Name Indication is protected from disclosure. There are still many ways an attacker might infer it. Even in an idealized deployment, the protection is limited to an anonymity set consisting of all the Encrypted-ClientHello-enabled server domains supported by a given client-facing server that share an ECH configuration. An attacker who can enumerate this set can always guess the encrypted name with a probability of at least 1/K, where K is the number of domains in the set. Some attackers may achieve much greater accuracy using traffic analysis, popularity weighting and other mechanisms.

Encrypted ClientHello ensures that TLS does not disclose the name, but the same information is also present in the DNS queries used to resolve the server's hostname. This specification does not conceal the server name from the DNS resolver. If DNS messages are sent between the client and the resolver without authenticated encryption, an attacker on that path can also learn the destination server name, and a similar attack applies if the client can be linked to a request from the resolver to a DNS authority.

An attacker who can prevent SVCB resolution can deny clients any associated security benefits. A hostile recursive resolver can always deny service to SVCB queries, and network intermediaries can often prevent resolution as well, even when the client and the recursive resolver validate DNSSEC and use a secure transport. These downgrade attacks can prevent a client from being aware that ech is configured, which could result in the client sending the ClientHello in cleartext. To prevent downgrades, the Service Bindings specification recommends that clients abandon the connection attempt when such an attack is detected.
sections.plainLanguage: Four limits are worth knowing. A record set that offers the parameter on some servers but not others lets an attacker block the protected ones and force the client onto an unprotected one. The name is hidden only among the domains that share the same configuration, so an attacker who lists them can still guess it. The name is still visible in the DNS query, so it is not hidden from the resolver. And an attacker who blocks the DNS lookup can stop the client from ever learning that protection was available.

messages.label: RESOLVE
messages.note: The client looks up the HTTPS or SVCB record for the name.

messages.label: HTTPS RECORD
messages.note: The record carries the ech parameter with the server's ECH configuration.

messages.label: OUTER CLIENTHELLO
messages.note: The outer ClientHello is encrypted and names no service in the clear.

messages.label: HANDSHAKE
messages.note: The server reads the inner ClientHello, whose Server Name Indication names the real service.

viz.caption: The three rules the document sets for clients

items.title: No fallback
items.text: If SVCB resolution succeeded and every endpoint has an ech parameter, the client must not fall back to a direct connection.

items.title: Wait for the lookup
items.text: A client that supports ECH must not send any TLS ClientHello until SVCB resolution has completed.

items.title: Inner ClientHello only
items.text: The Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation rules and the Server Name Indication apply to the inner ClientHello.

viz.caption: A domain reachable only with ECH (RFC 9848, Figure 5)

data.title: Zone file for secret.example.
data.code:
$ORIGIN secret.example. ; High confidentiality zone
www     3600 IN HTTPS 1 backend ech=ABC... mandatory=ech
backend 300  IN A     192.0.2.1
                    AAAA  2001:db8::1

viz.caption: What the encryption does not hide

cells: An intermediary can block the endpoints that support ECH and force the client onto one that does not
The name can be guessed with a probability of at least 1/K, where K is the number of domains sharing the configuration
The server name is still visible in the DNS query, so this document does not hide it from the resolver
Stopping the DNS lookup can stop the client from learning that ECH was configured at all
